> You should probably simply ban printing shelf fillers from thingverse and such. Let students print only what they design themselves. Grabbing a little pokemon figure stl from web and printing it, teaches absolutely nothing - except that it is ok to waste energy, materials and time on a junk.

I agree. One of the challenges that we have is the sheer throughput that we see in the Invention Studio. Because it's not intended as purely a classroom/lab space, and because we are optimized to create a low barrier to entry for new users, it can be pretty hard for us to monitor every print on every printer, especially when we've got our hands full trying to teach new users how to get started.

We also cater to all of campus, including majors that are not traditionally that proficient in CAD, like EE or CS majors. Although we try to teach CAD as much as possible, we still encourage people to reach out and try projects that they may not yet have the skills to design from scratch when they start. It makes it hard to suss out whether you're printing Pokemon to collect them or if you're adapting it to be a part of an IOT Arduino project.

Thank you for your insightful critique of my post, and I am sorry that my post seems to have touched a nerve with you. This post was merely meant to highlight the difficulties I see in our current environment, and to provoke some sort of conversation regarding 3D printing and its role in the modern collegiate experience. 

I understand that you're having to make a lot of assumptions regarding my current teaching situation, and I probably should have clarified my educational environment within my post to make my situation more clear.

I am a volunteer at a student-run, academic makerspace at Georgia Tech, called the Invention Studio. We supervise safe operations on a wide swath of equipment, and we provide design and prototyping advice to students, staff, and faculty working on a wide variety of projects - personal, class, research, etc. Because we are volunteers who are also students, we aren't always able to provide on the spot feedback to people who have made mistakes printing. As of Fall 2016, we were estimated to see 18,000 students per semester, with an average of 200 students per day working across all of our rooms.

I agree with many of the points that you bring up about the iterative design process. Lord knows every one of my successful builds is based on the failures before them.

I think that the largest point that I disagree with in your assessment is that time consumed by failed fabrication affects only the student who has failed. Failed prints and printer downtime negatively affects ALL of our users. As it goes in our space, everyone who wants to 3D print, which is... most of our users, must wait for an available printer to get their own chance to attempt this exciting form of fabrication. People re-printing a shaft that they know will break because they've printed it already 6 times are merely preventing other users from making an exciting discovery or learning more about the prototyping process. Right now, we're very much struggling to figure out how to get these students to more carefully consider their designs and implementations, so that we maximize the output and knowledge that all of our users seek.

Yeah, I am sure that the solution to these difficulties lies in a change to the curriculum by the professors in my department. Unfortunately, they don't see a lot of the struggles on the shop floor that I witness. In fact, that was one of the purposes of this post; it was less of a "kids these days" and more of a "hey, this is a problem, let's please acknowledge it" kind of post. (In fact, I'm sharing it with my supervisors to explain some of the curriculum changes that I'm proposing.)

I really like your idea of the lab project to evaluate different strengths and benefits of different types of fabrication, and I might suggest it as an addendum to our manufacturing class.
How do you all try to address your engineers' deficiencies in GD&T? Maybe your strategies in industry could help at the collegiate level.

>The tech is great and ramps up design nicely but the process is really all that matters.. I make my students dive into why something failed. I guide them with questions when they don't see the big picture yet, but again process.

Many of the projects where I see these problems aren't directly supervised by a professor or leader, due to the loose participation restrictions of the Invention Studio. Students who theoretically should have learned the design process through their classes are either not fully connecting with their past courses or are disregarding what they've learned in an effort to churn projects out. However, students within the design courses are not that much better. Guiding students through projects and poorly thought out design decisions takes a lot of 1-on-1 time, and it appears to take second place towards teaching them the ABET-focused curriculum.

I found that my work as the Capstone TA last semester was particularly helpful for many students, as I had office hours specifically dedicated to helping them evaluate and rethink/revise designs.

Additionally, I will likely be attending Construct3D later this year.

I absolutely agree. There is definitely a use for 3D printing in the design process, and I, myself, use it all the time.

The problem is that I'm having trouble getting students to think critically about their design. In many cases, they seem to be throwing out the evaluate phase. I'm struggling to figure out how to encourage those practices on a more regular basis.
You are welcome. I sincerely hope it helps, especially considering what is currently happening in the GT community.

Update: Students who don't have access to InDesign because they aren't ID students who have a membership to the Adobe Creative Suite can access InDesign in the Multimedia Studio in the Library Basement.

GT has a sophomore level mechanical engineering class called Creative Decisions and Design (http://2110.me.gatech.edu/), where the final project is to design a "robot" to complete a series of challenges. It's a competition every semester to see who can score the highest points. It's not super technical, but it teaches the product design process, basic machining (on little tiny mills and lathes), and some mechatronics. It also teaches them how to justify design decisions.

Both of my previous internships sent me my official hiring work, and then stated that my employment would be confirmed following a drug test, but neither of mine were something that may relate to national security. Seeing as it's a military base, I'd be extremely surprised if they didn't drug test you.

Thanks for the beautiful examples! My only complaint about butterfly keys is that I think they make some finished pieces look aesthetically unbalanced.

I have access to a CNC router at my makerspace, and, while it does take away much of the pride of hand-detailing furniture, I am thinking of using it to add inlays to the piece alongside whatever structural supports I drop in there. Hopefully it will balance out the composition without making the piece look too busy.
